Laser therapy (e.g., pulsed dye laser) can lighten the stain but does not affect neurological disease.
faq.q: Can the facial stain be treated?

faq.a: It can worsen cognitive outcomes and interacts with many other drugs.
faq.q: Why avoid phenobarbital in these patients?

exam: What bedside sign would prompt you to suspect Sturge‑Weber in a child with seizures? — Look for a unilateral port‑wine stain in the V1/V2 distribution.
How would you confirm leptomeningeal involvement when MRI is unavailable? — Obtain a CT head; tram‑track calcifications support the diagnosis.
A child with Sturge‑Weber presents with refractory seizures; what is the next step? — Initiate ICU‑level seizure management and consider adding low‑dose aspirin after ruling out contraindications.
Which antiepileptic drug is preferred and why? — Levetiracetam, because it has minimal enzyme induction and fewer cognitive side effects.
What ocular complication should be screened for and how? — Glaucoma; perform tonometry and fundoscopy at each ophthalmology visit.
Distinguish Sturge‑Weber from tuberous sclerosis on exam. — Sturge‑Weber has a facial port‑wine stain; tuberous sclerosis shows ash‑leaf spots and facial angiofibromas.
Explain why aspirin may be used despite bleeding risk. — Low‑dose aspirin can reduce thrombotic events in leptomeningeal angiomas; use only if no bleeding contraindication.
What long‑term multidisciplinary follow‑up is essential? — Regular neurology, ophthalmology, physiotherapy and developmental assessments.
ai.title: Sturge-Weber Syndrome
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: A neurocutaneous disorder with facial port‑wine stain, leptomeningeal angiomas and neurological sequelae. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by imaging. Management focuses on seizure control and preventing complications.

b: Diagnosis is clinical; MRI with contrast confirms leptomeningeal angioma.
Absence of systemic vascular malformations distinguishes it from other neuro‑cutaneous syndromes.
sections.p: Sturge‑Weber syndrome is a sporadic congenital phakomatosis characterised by a facial capillary malformation (port‑wine stain) in the trigeminal distribution, ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomas and ocular involvement.

b: Mild: isolated facial stain, no seizures.
Moderate: seizures or mild visual impairment.
Severe: refractory epilepsy, hemiparesis, glaucoma, cognitive delay.
sections.p: Severity is graded by neurological involvement and ocular complications.

b: Sporadic mutation – no inheritance.
Associated with other vascular malformations (e.g., cerebral cavernous malformation).
sections.p: A somatic activating mutation in the GNAQ gene (c.548G>A) during embryogenesis leads to abnormal vascular development.

b: Port‑wine stain follows V1/V2 distribution.
Seizures often focal, may become generalized.
Glaucoma presents with photophobia, tearing, raised intra‑ocular pressure.
sections.p: Typical presentation in infancy or early childhood includes a facial port‑wine stain, seizures, developmental delay and possible glaucoma.
Imaging and ophthalmic assessment confirm the diagnosis and guide management.

t.b: Detects leptomeningeal angioma; shows gyriform enhancement and cortical calcifications – confirms neurovascular involvement.
Shows tram‑track calcifications; useful where MRI not accessible.
Screens for glaucoma; elevated intra‑ocular pressure requires urgent referral.
Identifies epileptiform activity; guides antiepileptic choice.

b: Refractory status epilepticus – requires ICU care.
Progressive hemiparesis or stroke‑like episodes.
Uncontrolled glaucoma – risk of irreversible blindness.
sections.p: Complications can be life‑threatening or cause permanent disability.

b: First‑line seizure control with broad‑spectrum antiepileptics (e.g., levetiracetam) – chosen for minimal drug interactions.
Avoid enzyme‑inducing AEDs (e.g., phenobarbital) that may worsen cognitive outcome.
Topical beta‑blocker (timolol) or prostaglandin analogues for glaucoma; surgery if pressure uncontrolled.
Low‑dose aspirin (if no contraindication) may reduce stroke‑like episodes by inhibiting platelet aggregation.
Physiotherapy and developmental support for motor/cognitive delay.
sections.p: Treat the neurological and ocular manifestations while monitoring for complications.

b: Neurology review every 3–6 months; adjust AEDs as needed.
Ophthalmology every 6 months; monitor intra‑ocular pressure.
Neuro‑imaging every 2–3 years to assess progression.
Counselling families about seizure safety and developmental milestones.
Klippel‑Trénaunay syndrome – limb overgrowth and venous malformations, no leptomeningeal angioma.
Neurofibromatosis type 1 – café‑au‑lait spots, neurofibromas, not port‑wine stain.
Tuberous sclerosis – ash‑leaf spots, cortical tubers, seizures but different skin lesions.
sections.p: Other neuro‑cutaneous syndromes may share cutaneous or neurological features.

b: Normal CT does not exclude leptomeningeal angioma; MRI is required.
Mildly elevated intra‑ocular pressure can be missed without tonometry.
sections.p: Certain investigations may be falsely reassuring.

whenToSeekHelp: New onset seizures or status epilepticus
Sudden visual loss or severe eye pain
